verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, with stringed instruments, a maskil of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the singers, to be played on strings: a song of insight, from David.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a stage direction, not part of the prayer. In the Hebrew numbering it counts as verse 1; the KJV prints it as an unnumbered heading and starts counting at the next verse, so every KJV number in this psalm is one lower than the Hebrew. 'Choirmaster' (מְנַצֵּחַ) is a temple music officer, and the strings (נְגִינוֹת) tell the performers that this lament is to be sung, not murmured. The KJV leaves 'Maschil' as an untranslated label; it names a type of poem, usually taken as an 'instruction' or a skillful composition. The early readers in the packet (Radak, Meiri, Malbim) attach this psalm to David's flight from Absalom and Ahithophel's betrayal; that setting is their reading, and the psalm itself never names it.

philological_notes.note: A heading term, from a root meaning 'to be wise, to have insight'. Its exact sense is uncertain: a teaching song, a skillfully made song, or a meditation. It is kept untranslated in the literal layer.
'To the one who leads (the music)'. The root also means 'to excel, to be pre-eminent', hence 'overseer' (YLT) and 'chief Musician' (KJV).

verses.translation_literal: Give ear, God, [to] my prayer, and do not hide yourself from my supplication.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen, God. Bend your ear to my prayer, and do not turn your face away from my plea.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with two commands in a row, which is not rudeness but the way an ancient petitioner approached a king: you call for a hearing before you state the case. 'Give ear' is literally 'make an ear', a physical picture of God leaning in, and Ibn Ezra and Meiri both note that the ear is borrowed from human anatomy as a way of speaking. The second line asks God not to hide, a standard image for a king or judge who turns away and refuses to see a petitioner (Metzudat David: 'do not hide yourself from hearing my plea'). The prayer (תְּפִלָּה) and the supplication (תְּחִנָּה) are a pair: Malbim sees in them the outpouring of the soul and the request for further needs. The KJV is accurate here; its only slip is the archaic 'thyself', which hides that the verb is a reflexive 'hide yourself'.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive verb: 'do not hide yourself, do not make yourself invisible'. It pictures God turning away to avoid a petitioner, as one avoids a beggar.
A plea for grace or favour, from the root 'to be gracious'. The petitioner has no claim, only an appeal to mercy.

verses.translation_literal: Pay attention to me and answer me; I am restless in my complaint and I am in uproar.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear me. Answer me. I cannot be still; I pace inside my own complaint, and my voice will not settle.
verses.directors_commentary: Two more commands, now sharper: 'pay attention' and 'answer', since in this world hearing without acting is no help. Then the man describes himself, and the Hebrew picks two unusual verbs: אָרִיד, 'I am restless' (as in Lam 3:19, 'my wandering'), and אָהִימָה, 'I am in uproar', from a root that gives the sound of a crowd. Both are physical: the speaker cannot sit, cannot be quiet. The KJV's 'I mourn' and 'make a noise' is loose; 'noise' is closer to the Hebrew than 'mourn', and the BBE's 'made low in sorrow' loses the restlessness altogether. 'Complaint' (שִׂיחַ) is not whining but speech poured out before God, as in Psalm 102:1. Rashi reads אָרִיד as 'I lament in my trouble' and cites Judges 11:37, where Jephthah's daughter says she will 'go down' to the mountains; Menachem, he reports, took it as 'rule', which makes no sense here. The performer should play a man who starts the sentence kneeling and finishes it on his feet.

philological_notes.note: Probably 'to roam restlessly' (as in Jer 2:31, Hos 12:1); related in sound to the root 'to go down' (ירד), a link Rashi and Ibn Ezra both draw. A man who cannot settle, in body and voice.
'My musing, my speech, my complaint': talk poured out, usually before God. It carries the idea of rehearsing one's troubles aloud.
Cohortative of a root meaning 'to murmur, to roar, to be in tumult' (compare המון, 'crowd'). Meiri compares it to ואהמה. It describes the noise of distress.

verses.translation_literal: From the voice of an enemy, from the face of the pressure of a wicked one, for they make iniquity totter down upon me, and in anger they are hostile to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is the enemy's voice that does it, that shout I cannot shut out; it is the wicked man's weight pressing on my chest. They tip their wrongs down over me, one on another, and what drives them is anger, plain and hot, and it has my name in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verses 2–3 end the opening complaint, and this verse gives its reason: the man is not shouting for nothing, he is under siege. Three pressures are named, a voice, a squeeze and a rage, and each is sound or weight rather than blade. The actor should play a man who is still being spoken at. Tradition fills in the story: Rashi names Doeg and Ahithophel (the informer of 1 Sam 22 and the counsellor of 2 Sam 15–17), who 'tip the scales' with iniquities against David and so make his blood permitted; Radak and Meiri read the enemy as Absalom and the wicked one as Ahithophel. 'Pressure' (עָקָה) is a rare noun; Rashi glosses it as narrowness and Metzudat Zion ties it to מוּעָקָה in Ps 66:11, a vice or snare.

The verb יָמִיטוּ is the knot of the verse, and the old commentators split on it. Ibn Ezra derives it from מוט, 'to totter', as in 'his hand falters' (Lev 25:35), here in the causative: they make wrong come tottering down on me. Radak takes it as 'incline, tilt' (they tilt falsehood toward me), and Meiri notes another reading, 'they bring it upon me' with a false and empty charge. Metzudat David reads it as 'trouble': they bring toil and weariness. The KJV's 'cast iniquity upon me' is a fair guess at the image, but it is smoother than the Hebrew, which has a load slipping and tipping over onto the speaker. And 'hate' for יִשְׂטְמוּנִי is flat; the verb is the one used of Esau's grudge against Jacob (Gen 27:41), a hostility that keeps its anger and stores it. Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David both read it as 'bearing a grudge'.

philological_notes.note: A Hiphil of מוט, 'to totter, shake, slip': 'they make [iniquity] totter down upon me'. Ibn Ezra reads it as from the root of 'his hand falters' (Lev 25:35) and takes the object 'iniquity' as the thing made to fall. Radak and Meiri read it as 'incline, tilt' (to bring something upon someone, falsehood or wrong). Metzudat David has 'trouble, toil'. Rashi's paraphrase (they tip the scales with iniquities) is nearer to the tilting sense.
'Pressure, squeezing', a hapax in this form. Rashi glosses it as 'narrowness'; Metzudat Zion says it is the Targum's word for 'trouble' and relates it to מוּעָקָה (Ps 66:11).

'They hold a grudge against me', the verb of Esau's hatred (Gen 27:41). It is a stored, ongoing hostility, which is why the KJV's 'hate' loses some of the force. Metzudat Zion links it to that Genesis verse.

token_glosses.gloss: from the face of, because of

verses.translation_literal: My heart writhes within me, and the terrors of death have fallen on me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart twists inside my chest like a woman in labor, and the terrors of death have dropped on me out of the dark.
verses.directors_commentary: The body takes over. The verb יָחִיל is the one used for labor pains and for the shaking of the earth, so 'is sore pained' (KJV, ASV) is correct in direction but thin: the heart is writhing, wringing itself. Radak and Meiri both note the link to a woman in childbirth (Ps 48:7). 'Within me' (בְּקִרְבִּי) is the inner organs, not just the chest, which makes the pain gut-deep. Then the 'terrors of death' fall: אֵימוֹת מָוֶת are not fears of dying someday but the dread that death itself sends ahead of it. The verb 'fall' is used for something dropping from above, and the KJV 'are fallen upon' keeps that. Ibn Ezra compares it to the terror of hearing a lion roar. Malbim reads the fear as a reaction to sudden news and the fear of being killed, which fits the traditional setting but is not required by the text.

philological_notes.note: To writhe or tremble in pain, as in labor. The same verb is used of the earth shaking and of a woman giving birth.
'Terrors of death': the dread cast by death before it arrives. The same word, אֵימָה, is used of the terror that fell on Abram in Gen 15:12.

verses.translation_literal: Fear and trembling come into me, and shuddering covers me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fear walks in, and trembling with it; and then the shuddering comes down over me like a cloak and I am hidden inside it.
verses.directors_commentary: Three words for terror in a row, each a step further inward and outward. Fear (יִרְאָה) 'comes into' the man; trembling (רַעַד) comes with it; and then פַּלָּצוּת, a rare, strong word for a shudder that grips the whole body, 'covers' him. The verb 'cover' (כָּסָה) is the same one used for clothing and for a flood covering the land, so the horror is a garment he cannot take off. Ibn Ezra puts it simply: fear is in the heart and trembling is in the body. Radak and Meiri treat the second and third words as synonyms; Malbim notes that the shudder is the one that seizes a person at the point of death. The KJV 'horror hath overwhelmed me' is serviceable but loses the image of a cloak: the Hebrew says that dread has dressed him.

philological_notes.note: A shuddering, a convulsive horror. It is rare and strong (compare Isa 21:4, 'shuddering has terrified me').
'And it covered me': the same verb as for clothing or a flood. The terror is something that wraps him. Metzudat David calls it a figure of speech for how completely trembling covered his body.

verses.translation_literal: And I said, Who will give me wings like the dove? I would fly away and I would settle.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I said it, out loud, to no one: who will give me wings, like the dove's? I would rise and fly, and I would find somewhere to land and stay.
verses.directors_commentary: The most famous line in the psalm, and the whole scene turns here from pain to escape. 'Who will give me' (מִי יִתֶּן לִי) is the standard Hebrew wish, a prayer without an addressee; 'Oh that I had' in the KJV gets the sense but turns a question into an exclamation. The Hebrew says אֵבֶר, a flight feather or pinion, which Ibn Ezra and Radak render as 'wing' (Aramaic כנף); the KJV's 'wings' fine. The dove is the weak bird that is still the fastest to escape, a bird of the town that yet flees to cliffs, and Ibn Ezra adds that it is the bird that kings use to carry their letters. The verbs matter: 'I would fly' and 'I would settle' (אֶשְׁכֹּנָה) are cohortatives, a wish stated as a plan, and the second is not 'be at rest' as in the KJV but the verb for dwelling, for pitching a tent; a person who wants a place to live. Malbim, quoting the Tosafists, notes that a dove can fly with one wing and settle on the other, a joke about wanting both to go and to stay.

philological_notes.note: A pinion or flight feather, a wing. Ibn Ezra renders it as the Aramaic 'wing'; Metzudat Zion compares Job 39:26, 'the hawk soars (יֶאֱבַר־נֵץ)'.
'And I would settle, dwell.' The verb of tenting and residence, not simply of rest; the speaker wants a home, not a pause.

verses.translation_literal: Look, I would go far away, to flee; I would lodge in the wilderness. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: See how far I would go. I would run until the last house was gone, and sleep in the wilderness. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The dream picks up pace: הִנֵּה, 'look!', turns the wish into a picture of what he would do. 'Far' (אַרְחִיק) and 'to flee' (נְדֹד) are doubled for emphasis, and the wilderness here is the opposite of the city: no walls, no people, no neighbors. The KJV 'wander far off' is close, but נָדַד is to flee or to be driven, not to stroll. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the point is leaving settled land, where a wanderer can at least be safe from men. 'Lodge' (אָלִין) is the verb for spending the night, so he is thinking of one night at a time and not a permanent home, which sits oddly with 'settle' in the last verse and shows the speaker contradicting himself. The Targum, which turns it into 'forever', shows the early readers felt that tension. 'Selah' marks a musical or liturgical pause of uncertain meaning, perhaps an instrumental interlude: after this wish, the music stops.

philological_notes.note: A term of the psalm tradition, perhaps a pause, interlude or lifting of voices; its meaning is lost. Malbim treats it as marking the end of a thought.
'I would lodge, spend the night.' It is the verb of staying overnight, not of living somewhere.

verses.translation_literal: I would hurry [to] a place of escape for myself, from the rushing wind, from the storm.
verses.translation_dramatic: I would race to a shelter of my own, out of the wind that tears and the storm that will not let go.
verses.directors_commentary: The wilderness is now not a place of loneliness but of shelter, because the thing he flees is a storm. The 'wind' is סֹעָה, a hapax legomenon (found nowhere else); Rashi compares it to 'it uproots like a tree' and 'they set out' (as of journeying), and Radak says plainly that the word has no companion in the Bible and must be explained by its place here. The KJV 'windy storm and tempest' is a doubled phrase that repeats 'storm' for emphasis; the Hebrew is two items, a wind and a storm (סַעַר), with the same two-step rhythm as 'fear and trembling'. 'A place of escape' (מִפְלָט) is not a hiding place but an escape route, the way out. The wind and storm are an image of his enemies (Rashi, Metzudat David); Malbim places the line at the moment of the later advice about the night attack. The KJV 'I would hasten my escape' loses the 'for me' (לִי), a dative of interest: a refuge of my own.

philological_notes.note: 'Rushing, sweeping'; occurs only here. Ibn Ezra reads it as a shortened 'נוסעה', 'traveling', and Metzudat Zion compares 'a wind moved' (Num 11:31).
A way of escape, a rescue. The root means to slip away or be delivered.

verses.translation_literal: Swallow up, O Lord, divide their tongue, for I have seen violence and strife in the city.
verses.translation_dramatic: Undo them, Lord. Take their counsel apart; split their tongue so it will not speak as one. For I have seen it with my own eyes: violence in the streets and strife inside the walls, and the city does not sleep.
verses.directors_commentary:
The wish for wings is over. Verses 7–9 imagine flight; here the man turns back to the city and prays against it, abruptly. 'Divide' (פַּלַּג) is the word at the root of the Babel story, where the tongue is divided and the plan falls apart (Gen 10:25; 11:1–9): Ibn Ezra reads the prayer as asking that the plotters meet the fate of the generation of the dispersion, 'for all of them gathered in the city to do me violence'. The tradition makes it David's prayer against Ahithophel (Radak, Meiri, Malbim; compare 2 Sam 15:31): break their agreement, and their counsel falls apart. Metzudat David says the point is that no man will understand his neighbour's speech, so that their wicked plan is cancelled. Rashi reads 'divide their tongue' as 'separate it, so that no one will listen to them'.

The first verb is disputed. בַּלַּע looks like a Piel of בלע, 'swallow', and the KJV renders 'Destroy', which is not a softening, since Rashi (after Menachem), Meiri and both Metzudot read it as 'destroy, undo' (Meiri: 'ruin their counsel'). Radak adds the purpose: destroy them so that their counsel is confounded. STEPBible's 'confuse' reflects a different lexicon reading and is not what the old commentators say. The Lord is addressed as אֲדֹנָי, 'my Lord', not the name YHWH, a more personal, more urgent address. 'The city' is Jerusalem for Radak and Meiri. 'Violence' (חָמָס) is the sin that ends the flood world (Gen 6:11): wrong done to a neighbour with force and no regard for the law, and 'strife' is its quarrel at the courts and gates. Play both as things the speaker has watched, not heard of.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of בלע, whose basic sense is 'swallow'. The old commentators read it as 'destroy, undo' (Rashi, citing Menachem and Lam 2:8; Meiri; Metzudat Zion). The pointing with patah is explained by Ibn Ezra as due to the guttural. 'Confuse' in STEPBible is a modern lexical reading that Radak echoes only as the aim of the destruction.

'Divide, split'. The same root as Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided (Gen 10:25), so the verb recalls Babel. Ibn Ezra reads it as a prayer that they meet the fate of the generation of the dispersion.

verses.translation_literal: By day and night they go around it on its walls; and wickedness and trouble are in its midst.
verses.translation_dramatic: Day and night they make their rounds along its walls, like sentries; and inside, wickedness and trouble have taken the middle of the city for themselves.
verses.directors_commentary: The city is described as a besieged place, but the guards are not soldiers: 'they' going round the walls are, in Rashi's reading, violence and strife themselves, personified as watchmen. The picture is a place whose protectors have been replaced by the things it should be protected from. Ibn Ezra draws it as a circle, with the walls as the circle line and 'wickedness and trouble' as the center point, which is exactly what 'in its midst' says. The KJV 'mischief and sorrow' is soft: אָוֶן is wickedness or harm, and עָמָל is toil, trouble, the sweat of oppression, not 'sorrow'. The walls were a city's pride and protection, the line between order and wilderness, which the speaker has just wished to flee into. The earlier verse put the wilderness as refuge; here the city, with walls, is the danger. Note that the pronoun for the city is feminine singular: the city is spoken of as a woman, in the usual way for a city (and the KJV's 'thereof' hides it).

philological_notes.note: 'They go around it': the verb of marching round a city (as at Jericho). In Rashi's reading the subject is the violence and strife of the previous verse.
Toil, trouble, the labor and misery of oppression. Not 'sorrow' as in the KJV; it is trouble made by or for others.

verses.translation_literal: Ruin [is] in its midst, and oppression and deceit do not depart from its public square.
verses.translation_dramatic: Ruin sits in its heart, and in the open square, where everyone passes, oppression and lies never move away.
verses.directors_commentary: The last verse of this window finishes the portrait of the city, moving from the walls to the center and then outward to the wide square (רְחוֹב), the place where a city's legal business, trade and gossip happened. This was where the elders sat at the gate and deals were witnessed, so corruption there means that justice itself is bad. 'Ruin' (הַוּוֹת) is plural, 'destructions', and Rashi and Radak gloss it as 'breakings, wreckage'. 'Does not depart' (לֹא יָמִישׁ) is a singular verb with two subjects: the two vices are felt as one thing, a stain that will not leave. The KJV 'wickedness' loses the plural of ruins, and 'deceit and guile' is a doubling in English where the Hebrew has two distinct things: תֹּךְ, 'oppression' or 'fraud' (its meaning is uncertain; Rashi derives it from 'striking', Radak from speaking one way with the mouth and another in the heart), and מִרְמָה, 'deceit'. The ASV's 'oppression' is nearer. Radak's reading, that people meet in the square to plot, puts the psalm back in its traditional setting, with the plotters discussing their plans in public.

philological_notes.note: Plural 'destructions, calamities'; Rashi glosses it as 'breakings', Radak as 'ruin and evil'. Not 'wickedness' as in the KJV, which belongs to אָוֶן.
Meaning uncertain: 'oppression, fraud'. Rashi derives it from a word for striking; Radak from deceit, a man whose mouth and heart do not match. Glossed 'oppression' here.
The wide open space of a city, the public square, where business and law were conducted; the KJV 'streets' is vaguer.

verses.translation_literal: For [it is] not an enemy [who] taunts me, and I [could] bear [it]; not [one who] hates me [who] has made himself great over me, and I [could] hide from him.
verses.translation_dramatic: It was no enemy who flung the insult. An enemy I could have borne; I would have swallowed the sting and walked on. It was no hater who reared himself up over me. From such a man I could have slipped away and hidden.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse sets up the sting of the next one by listing what David could have survived. In the ancient Near East an open enemy is a known quantity: you keep out of his reach, you wear the insult as a soldier wears a scar. The two imperfects (`yechareFeni`, `ve'esa'`) are best played as a rueful 'I could have...', not as a plain statement of the past. Notice the careful symmetry, taunt and endure, grow great and hide, and the shift from `'oyev` (enemy) to `meSan'i` (one who hates me): the second is a participle, the active hater, not a general foe.

The KJV makes the verse a little too formal with 'it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it': the Hebrew has no 'then', only an 'and' that the reader hears as a conditional. The verb `higdil`, 'made himself great', is the posture of arrogance and recalls the idiom 'magnify the mouth' (Radak glosses 'his mouth, to speak evil'). The BBE's 'one outside the number of my friends' is an interpretation, not a translation.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'grow great', here with 'al, 'over me': to make oneself big, to boast and lord it over someone. Radak adds 'with his mouth', as in Ezek 35:13.
Niphal 'I would hide myself': hiding is only possible from someone who does not already know where you are, so the next verse makes the speaker's friend the one person he cannot hide from.

verses.translation_literal: And you, a man [of] my rank, my intimate and my acquaintance.
verses.translation_dramatic: But it was you. You: a man of my own standing, my confidant, the one I knew and who knew me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The whole psalm turns on this verse, and it is a sentence without a verb: three fragments dropped like stones, 'you... a man... my equal'. The actor should break after 'And you'. `'enosh ke'erki` literally 'a man according to my valuation': someone I ranked as myself. Then two nouns of closeness: `'alluphi`, 'my intimate/chief', can mean the head of a clan (the 'chiefs' of Edom, Gen 36), and `meyuda'i`, 'my known one', is the person to whom one has disclosed oneself. Metzudat David and Radak take `'alluphi` as a minister or officer, which fits a court setting.

The KJV's 'my guide' reads `'alluphi` as 'one who leads' (from `'alaph`, 'teach'); the Hebrew is more likely 'intimate friend' (so the ASV 'companion' and Rashi). 'Mine equal' in the KJV is serviceable, but `'erekh` is a valuation, a price-tag: the speaker is saying 'I priced you as I price myself'.

philological_notes.note: 'According to my valuation, as I am assessed': from the root for setting in order, arranging, assessing a value (as in Lev 27 for the valuation of persons).
Attested both as 'chief, clan leader' and as 'close friend, intimate' (Prov 16:28; Mic 7:5). Metzudat Zion reads 'my chief' with Mic 7:5; the parallel with `meyuda'i` favours 'intimate'.

verses.translation_literal: Who together [we] made sweet counsel, in the house of God we walked about in a throng.
verses.translation_dramatic: We shared our secrets together, and they were sweet. We went up to the house of God, the two of us, among the pressing crowd.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is about sound and taste: `namtik sod`, 'we made counsel sweet', says the pleasure of shared confidences, the way two friends will savour a plan. `Sod` is not just advice; it is the circle of the intimate, the inner council (it is the word Jeremiah uses for the council of YHWH). Then comes a public scene: 'the house of God', in David's time the tent that housed the ark, later the Temple. `Ragesh` (here, a throng) is a rare, noisy word, the crowd as a hum or a roar, and Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion all read it as a company or crowd.

The KJV 'walked unto the house of God in company' turns the Hebrew locative 'in the house of God' into a destination and the crowd into 'company'; the picture is of pilgrims jostling through the court of a sanctuary. The friend was not only a private confidant but part of the shared worship of the community: his betrayal is also a profanation.

philological_notes.note: 'We made counsel sweet': the hiphil of 'be sweet'. `Sod` is the intimate circle or confidential counsel, not just a secret.
'In a throng, in noisy company': related to the verb in Ps 2:1, 'why do the nations rage (rag'shu)'. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion all take it as a crowd.

verses.translation_literal: May death be a creditor upon them; may they go down [to] Sheol alive; for evils [are] in their lodging, in their midst.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let death come down on them like a creditor to collect. Let them go down to Sheol while they still draw breath. For evil has taken a lodging among them, and made its home deep in their midst.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood breaks. The friend of the last three verses disappears and a curse in the plural surges up: 'them', his whole circle. It is an imprecation, but note what it asks for: not a battle but a sudden descent. 'Alive to Sheol' is the fate of Korah's company (Num 16:30, 'they went down alive into Sheol'), and the audience would hear that echo.

The first verb is a minefield. The written text (Ketiv) has `yashi`, the margin (Qere) `yashi'`. I read it as the language of debt: death as a creditor who comes to take what is owed, the sense given by Ibn Ezra (citing R. Moshe), Metzudat Zion (cf. Ps 89:23) and Malbim. Rashi hears a different verb, 'let God incite the angel of death against them', like the serpent who 'beguiled' Eve (Gen 3:13), and Menachem a third, 'let death be upon them'. The KJV's 'let death seize upon them' guesses at the sense and does not translate the word. The KJV's 'hell' for `she'ol` is a mistake of vocabulary: Sheol is the underworld of all the dead, not a place of fiery punishment, and 'quick' means 'alive'. `Meguram` is a sojourner's lodging, a place where one stays as a guest: evil is their lodger, and lives in their inner parts (`qerev`) too.

philological_notes.note: Written without aleph (`yashi`), read with it (`yashi'`). Rendered here as 'be a creditor' (from nasha, 'lend on debt', cf. Ps 89:23), the sense of Ibn Ezra's R. Moshe, Metzudat Zion and Malbim. Rashi instead reads 'incite, deceive' (cf. Gen 3:13), and Menachem 'there is' (yesh).

'Their lodging, sojourn': the place where someone lives as a guest; Rashi glosses 'their lodging', Metzudat Zion 'dwelling'. Radak takes it as 'their gathering-place' in Jerusalem, Ibn Ezra as 'their company'.

verses.translation_literal: I, to God I call; and YHWH, he will save me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I will call out to God, and the LORD will save me.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the curse, a single short breath. The pronoun comes first, `'ani`, 'as for me', setting the speaker against the plural 'them'. The verse switches the divine name: 'God' (`'Elohim`) for the calling, then YHWH, the covenant name, for the saving. The Hebrew is wonderfully plain, only six words, and should be spoken in a lower voice than the verses of anger around it.

The KJV 'the Lord shall save me' prints YHWH as 'the Lord' in small capitals in many editions, hiding that the name changes mid-verse. Note also the tenses: the first verb `'eqra'` is imperfect (I call, I keep calling), the second a hiphil imperfect of `yasha'`, 'to bring salvation', from the root of the name Joshua.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to be spacious, safe': 'he will bring me salvation', the root behind Joshua and Jesus.

verses.translation_literal: Evening and morning and noon[s] I will muse and I will murmur, and he heard my voice.
verses.translation_dramatic: At evening, at dawn, at the height of noon, I will pour out my complaint, and murmur like one who cannot be silent. And he heard my voice.
verses.directors_commentary:
The order is odd to a modern ear: evening, morning, noon. It follows the Hebrew day, which begins at sundown (Gen 1:5, 'there was evening and there was morning'), so the sequence is a day's cycle, and noon, the hottest hour, closes it. Rashi reads this as the three daily prayers (Berakhot 26b); that is later practice, but it is how the tradition heard it. The dual form `tzohorayim`, 'double light', is the noon sun at its height.

Both verbs are heavy: `'asicha`, 'I will muse, complain' and `'ehemeh`, 'I will moan, growl', the word used of doves and of the sea. The KJV's 'pray and cry aloud' makes it sound cleaner and more liturgical than the Hebrew, which is the sound of someone who cannot stop talking to God about his pain. And look at the last verb: `vayyishma'`, with a vav-consecutive, 'and he heard': past tense, as though the answer is already in. Radak and Meiri call this the prophetic past, speaking of a future certainty as accomplished.

philological_notes.note: 'I will muse, complain, speak out': used of anxious or lamenting speech, not of calm meditation (cf. Ps 55:3, 'esicha).
A vav-consecutive past, 'and he heard', after future verbs; Radak and Meiri explain it as the prophetic perfect.

verses.translation_literal: He ransomed in peace my life from [the] battle against me, for in many [they] were with me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has ransomed my life and brought it home in peace, out of the thick of the battle that closed around me, for many stood with me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tenses are the first problem: `padah` is a perfect, 'he has ransomed', again the certainty of faith spoken as fact. `Padah` is a market word, the price paid to free a slave or a firstborn; God is the one who pays. `Bashalom`, 'in peace', says the rescue leaves the speaker whole.

The second half is a puzzle that the commentators fight over. 'In many were they with me' reads awkwardly: Meiri notes the beth in `birabbim` may be pleonastic (as in Prov 9:5, 'eat of my bread'), and gives three readings: the many were against David; the many (angels, supporters) were on his side (2 Kings 6:16, 'more are with us than with them'); or it names all Israel who loved him (1 Sam 18:16, Rashi). Radak reads it as enemies (the many fought him), Ibn Ezra as angels. The KJV's 'for there were many with me' picks a side without saying so. The BBE's 'against me' picks the other. The Hebrew just says `'immadi`, 'at my side, with me', which is ambiguous in a way the translators erased. I leave the sense open in the literal and lean to the ally reading in the dramatic.

philological_notes.note: 'From the battle / from the approach': `qerav` is both 'battle' (Ps 144:1, Eccl 9:18) and 'nearness'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take 'battle'; Ibn Ezra and Meiri also allow 'from drawing near to touch me'.
The beth is a puzzle: 'for in/among many', 'for with many'. Meiri cites Prov 9:5 as a parallel for an expletive beth and offers three readings (enemies, helpers, 'all Israel').

verses.translation_literal: God will hear and answer them, and [the one] sitting [enthroned] from of old, Selah, who [have] no changes to them, and they do not fear God.
verses.translation_dramatic: God will hear, and God will answer them, the One who sits enthroned from before time began. Selah. In these men there is no change, and they do not fear God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar is tangled and every commentator reads it differently. `Ya'anem` could be from `'anah` 'to answer' (God will answer them) or from `'anah` 'to humble, bow down'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion take it as 'humble them' (cf. Ex 10:3, 'to humble yourself before me'), and Ibn Ezra gives a first view 'make them poor' and then prefers 'deal with them'; this is how the KJV's 'afflict' arises. The literal layer keeps 'answer'; the sense of a harsh answer is close either way.

`Yoshev qedem` is 'the one enthroned from of old'; `qedem` means both 'east' and 'ancient time', and the phrase is the title of a king long on his throne (Rashi: 'the king who sits of old'). Then the musical marker 'Selah', a pause. `Chaliphot` is 'changes', and the KJV's 'they have no changes' is correct but opaque. The commentators give three readings: no change of conduct, no turning from their ways (Meiri); no turn of fortune from good to bad (Ibn Ezra); no thought of their own passing, no dread of the day of death (Rashi, Metzudat David). All three agree on the last clause: 'they do not fear God'. The persecutors are fixed and unshaken, which is why judgment is certain.

philological_notes.note: From `'anah` 'answer', or from `'anah` 'humble, afflict'. Ibn Ezra first takes it from 'poor' (ani) and then prefers 'deal with them', as in 'we have not touched you'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read 'subdue them', comparing Ex 10:3; the KJV's 'afflict' follows them.

'Changes, successions', the root of the changes of clothing in Gen 45:22. Three readings: no change of conduct (Meiri); no turn of fortune from good to bad (Ibn Ezra); no thought of their own passing or death (Rashi, Metzudat David). Radak and one view in Meiri refer the clause to God, who does not change.

verses.translation_literal: He sent out his hands against his [men of] peace; he profaned his covenant.
verses.translation_dramatic: He stretched out his hands against the very ones who were at peace with him. He made a common thing of his covenant.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker returns to the betrayer, now as 'he'. `Shalach yadav`, 'sent out his hands', is the idiom for laying violent hands on someone (1 Sam 24:7 uses it for David's refusal to touch Saul). `Shelomav`, literally 'his peaces', is plainly 'his men of peace, his allies', as Ibn Ezra and Meiri note with the parallel `'ani tefillah` (Ps 109:4, 'I am prayer'). Rashi: 'he who was quiet and whole with him'.

The heart of the verse is the verb `chillel`, which the KJV renders 'broken'. The Hebrew is stronger: it means 'to profane, to make ordinary, to defile what was holy', and the ASV's 'profaned' is closer. A `berit` was a sworn treaty sealed with an oath before God, and here the betrayal is not a mere breach of contract but a sacrilege against the God who witnessed it, which is why this verse comes between two accounts of the house of God and divine judgment.

philological_notes.note: 'Against his peaces', i.e. men at peace with him, as in `'ani tefillah` 'I am prayer' (Ps 109:4). Meiri notes the alternative of reading it as shelemim (Gen 34:21).
'Profaned, desecrated': the opposite of making holy; used of breaking a covenant, a vow, a sanctuary or a name.

verses.translation_literal: Smooth [were] the creamy things of his mouth, and war [was] his heart; soft [were] his words, more than oil, and they [were] drawn [swords].
verses.translation_dramatic: His mouth was butter-smooth, and his heart was war. His words were softer than oil, and every one of them a drawn sword.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most famous image of the psalm, a double contrast, mouth against heart, oil against steel. The first line is about taste and feel (cream, smoothness), the second about sound (soft words) and then the blade. The form is chiastic: smooth mouth / war heart // soft words / drawn swords.

`Machma'ot` appears only here; the traditional reading (Rashi, Radak) is the plural of `chem'ah`, 'curd, butter', with an extra mem as a prefix, so 'smoother than butter' as in the KJV. YLT's 'sweeter than honey' is a different tradition. The word `qerav` is 'battle', and 'war was his heart' is bolder than the KJV's 'war was in his heart': the Hebrew has no 'in', the heart is the war. `Pitchot` is a rare word for swords (Mic 5:5, 'the land of Nimrod with its drawn blades'), so 'drawn swords' is right and fits Rashi's quotation of Menachem; Rashi's own alternative, an Aramaic term for a writ of excommunication, is clever but unlikely in a psalm.

philological_notes.note: A hapax: probably 'curds, butter' (`chem'ah`) with a prefixed mem, 'creamy things'; Rashi and Radak read 'smoother than butter'.
'Drawn swords', from the sense of opening or unsheathing; compare Mic 5:5 `bit'chehah`, and Ps 37:14 'the wicked have drawn the sword (`pat'chu`)'.

verses.translation_literal: Cast upon YHWH what he has given you, and he will sustain you; he will not give, for ever, a stumbling to the righteous.
verses.translation_dramatic: Throw it on the LORD, whatever he has laid on you, and he will hold you up. He will never let the righteous man stagger and fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice shifts: the psalmist now turns and speaks to himself, or to any righteous listener (Radak, Metzudat David), in the imperative. A porter's image lies behind it: `hashlekh` is a throw, a hurl, not a gentle laying down, as one swings a pack off the shoulder.

`Yehavkha` occurs only here in the Bible. The Talmud (Rashi, Radak, Meiri) takes it as 'your burden', and the KJV and ASV follow; Ibn Ezra reports a second view, 'what he has given you' (from `yahav`, to give, as YLT), your lot, and I keep this in the literal layer. `Yekhalkelkha` is a rare intensive for 'hold up, sustain' (cf. 1 Kings 8:27, the heavens 'cannot contain you'). `Mot` is a stagger, a slip of the foot (Rashi), and is the same word as in Ps 15:5, 'will never be moved'. The KJV 'suffer the righteous to be moved' uses 'suffer' in its old sense of 'allow'.

philological_notes.note: A hapax. Talmud, Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion: 'your burden'; Ibn Ezra's alternative: 'what he has given you'.
Pilpel of 'hold, contain, sustain': 'he will bear you up'. Rashi cites 1 Kgs 8:27.

verses.translation_literal: And you, God, you will bring them down to the well of the pit; men of bloods and deceit will not halve their days; and I, I will trust in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, O God, will bring them down into the well of the pit. Men of blood and of lies will not live out half their days. And I will trust in you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends as it began, with the contrast of 'you' and 'I', and the actor should deliver 'and I' quietly after the thundering of the curse. `Be'er shachat`, 'the well of the pit', pairs a well with `shachat`, the pit of the grave, a cistern-like shaft; the KJV's 'pit of destruction' takes `shachat` from the root 'to ruin', which the word can also hint at, but the sense here is the grave (Metzudat Zion: 'grave'; Radak and Meiri also allow Gehenna).

`Anshei damim`, 'men of bloods', is plural: bloodshed in the sense of violent deeds, not a single killing. Such men 'will not halve their days' (`lo yechetzu`): they will not reach half of the span measured out to them (Metzudat David), or in Ibn Ezra's words, their number of days will not be filled. The KJV's 'live out half their days' is right. To an ancient reader, to die in mid-life was the mark of divine disfavour. The ending is quiet: the last word, `bakh`, 'in you', is one syllable.

philological_notes.note: 'Well of the pit': the grave or the underworld. Metzudat Zion glosses `shachat` as 'grave'; Radak and Meiri allow Gehenna.
'They will not halve their days': they will not reach half of their allotted days (Metzudat David), or their number of days will not be filled (Ibn Ezra).
